Against the Imperial Judiciary: A Case for Popular Constitutionalism

The Case for Abolishing Judicial Supremacy

In 1803, in the case of Marbury v. Madison, the Supreme Court of the United States asserted for itself a power that the Constitution nowhere explicitly grants: the authority to strike down acts of the coordinate political branches as unconstitutional. This judicial coup, executed with breathtaking confidence and questionable legitimacy, has shaped American governance for over two centuries. Today, an unelected body of nine individuals—appointed for life, answerable to no constituency, and removable by no democratic process—holds the final say on questions of fundamental rights, the structure of government, the scope of federal power, and the meaning of our foundational charter. It is time to acknowledge what constitutional scholars from Jefferson to Kramer have long argued: judicial review as we know it is a structural defect in American democracy, and the Supreme Court as it currently exists is an undemocratic institution that should be abolished or radically reconstituted.

The Democratic Deficit

The most fundamental problem with the Supreme Court is simple and inescapable: it is profoundly anti-democratic. In a republic founded on the principle that government derives its just powers from the consent of the governed, nine lawyers who serve for life and cannot be recalled wield a power that overrides the will of the people's elected representatives. This is not a minor structural quirk—it is a contradiction at the heart of the American constitutional order.

Consider what the Court does. It can invalidate laws passed by Congress, the directly elected representatives of the American people. It can strike down legislation approved by a president who won a national election. It can effectively veto policy decisions made through the ordinary democratic process, substituting its own judgment for that of elected officials. The only check on this power is the extraordinarily difficult process of constitutional amendment, which requires supermajorities in both houses of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of state legislatures—a threshold effectively impossible to meet in our polarized era.

The framers of the Constitution were not naïve about the dangers of unchecked power. They designed a system of checks and balances, but the genius of their design was that the branches they created were all ultimately accountable to the people. The president faces elections. Members of Congress face elections repeatedly. Even the Senate, originally appointed by state legislatures, was democratized. Only the judiciary was insulated from popular control, and only the judiciary was never given the explicit constitutional authority to invalidate the acts of the other branches.

The Myth of Constitutional Grounding

Defenders of judicial review often claim that it was always implicit in the Constitution, that the framers clearly intended the courts to have this power. This claim does not withstand serious historical scrutiny. The constitutional text contains no provision establishing judicial review. The framers debated the matter extensively in the Philadelphia Convention, and proposals to give the courts a role in invalidating legislation were explicitly considered and rejected. Alexander Hamilton's famous defense of judicial review in Federalist No. 78 was the work of one influential commentator, not a binding statement of constitutional meaning.

The Supreme Court itself did not assert the power of judicial review until 1803, more than a decade after ratification. For the first century of American constitutional history, the power of judicial review was a contested and uncertain doctrine. The idea that it is a sacred, original feature of American constitutionalism is historical revisionism.

Moreover, the Court's assertion of this power in Marbury was, as constitutional scholar Larry Kramer has argued in The People Themselves, an act of judicial overreach that contradicted the more democratic vision of the Constitution's ratifiers. Many of those who supported the Constitution believed that the people themselves, acting through their representatives, would be the ultimate interpreters of its meaning. The early practice of constitutional interpretation was far more pluralistic, with multiple branches and even the people themselves playing interpretive roles. The Court's monopolization of constitutional interpretation is a historical accident, not a constitutional necessity.

A Record of Failure

Even if one were inclined to accept the principle of judicial review in theory, the actual record of the Supreme Court offers little justification for entrusting it with such immense power. The Court has a long and ignominious history of decisions that were not only wrong but morally repugnant, and that were eventually overruled only after great damage had been done.

In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), the Court declared that Black Americans could not be citizens, helping to bring the nation to the brink of civil war. In Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), the Court enshrined the doctrine of "separate but equal," legitimizing decades of state-sponsored segregation. In Korematsu v. United States (1944), the Court upheld the internment of Japanese Americans during World War II. In Buck v. Bell (1927), Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes infamously wrote that "three generations of imbeciles are enough" in upholding compulsory sterilization.

Even more fundamentally, the Court has reversed itself on critical constitutional questions with embarrassing frequency. Plessy was overturned by Brown. Decisions protecting economic regulation were overturned in 1937. Doctrines of separate but equal gave way to integration. The Court's own evolving jurisprudence on issues ranging from the Equal Protection Clause to the Commerce Clause demonstrates that its interpretations are not fixed or objective but contingent and shifting.

This is not an argument for any particular policy position—it is an argument about institutional design. If the Court is capable of dramatically changing its mind on fundamental questions, and if the people, through their elected representatives and constitutional amendments, are capable of eventually correcting the Court's errors, then why should the Court stand between the people and the resolution of these questions in the first place? The bottleneck of waiting for five out of nine unelected lawyers to agree with the democratic consensus produces years or decades of unjust rule in the interim.

The Politicization Problem

Defenders of the Court often claim that it is a neutral, apolitical institution that decides cases on the basis of legal principle. This claim is increasingly difficult to sustain. The contemporary confirmation process for Supreme Court justices is a heavily politicized spectacle, with nominees' judicial philosophies dissected along partisan lines. Justices are routinely chosen based on their perceived views on contested political issues—abortion, gun rights, regulatory power, religious liberty. Once appointed, justices often vote along the ideological lines that were apparent at their confirmation hearings.

The Court has become, in effect, a quasi-legislative body whose members are chosen through a backdoor political process, serve for life, and cannot be removed or overruled by ordinary democratic means. This is a worse system than a straightforwardly political process, because it conceals the political nature of the decisions behind a veneer of legal objectivity.

Consider the alternative: a system in which constitutional questions are decided by elected representatives, who must face the voters and defend their judgments. Such representatives would be subject to continuous democratic accountability. Their decisions would be openly debated in the public sphere. Voters could evaluate their representatives' constitutional views alongside their other policy positions. There would be no pretense that constitutional interpretation is something other than the political judgment it actually is.

Popular Constitutionalism

A better system would recognize that constitutional interpretation is an inherently democratic function that should be exercised by democratic institutions. There are several possible models:

Legislative Supremacy: Under this model, Congress and the state legislatures would have the final say on constitutional questions. Constitutional amendments could be passed by simple or supermajority votes of the legislature, with executive concurrence, and would be subject to judicial review only in extreme cases involving procedural violations.

Popular Referendum: The most radically democratic model would allow the people themselves to decide constitutional questions through direct vote. The Swiss system of popular initiatives and referendums provides a model for how direct democracy can coexist with representative institutions.

Sunset Provisions: Constitutional provisions could be designed to expire after a fixed period unless reaffirmed by democratic action, ensuring that the constitutional order evolves with the consent of each generation.

None of these models is perfect. But all of them share the virtue of placing ultimate authority over constitutional questions in the hands of those who are constitutionally sovereign in a democratic republic: the people.

Addressing the Counterargument

The strongest objection to popular constitutionalism is that it leaves minorities vulnerable to majoritarian tyranny. If constitutional rights are determined by majority vote, the argument goes, then unpopular minorities will be at the mercy of the majority, and rights that we now take for granted—racial equality, religious freedom, LGBT rights—could be stripped away by popular referendum.

This objection has some force, but it is weaker than it appears. First, it assumes that the current system actually protects minority rights effectively, an assumption undermined by the Court's long history of permitting injustices ranging from slavery to segregation. Second, it assumes that the only way to protect minority rights is through judicial review, when in fact democratic constitutions can include explicit anti-majoritarian features—such as supermajority requirements for certain types of legislation, federalism protections, or entrenched individual rights—that operate without the need for a powerful unelected judiciary.

Moreover, the minority rights argument proves too much. If we are willing to overrule democratic majorities in cases involving constitutional rights, we must confront the question of who decides what those rights are. Allowing nine unelected lawyers to override the considered judgments of elected representatives and the people themselves is hardly an obvious improvement over the alternative of democratic decision-making.

Conclusion

The American system of judicial supremacy is a historical accident, not a constitutional mandate. It is anti-democratic in structure, prone to serious error in practice, and increasingly politicized in operation. The arguments for popular constitutionalism are not new—they have been advanced by some of the most serious minds in American political thought, from Thomas Jefferson to Abraham Lincoln to contemporary scholars like Larry Kramer, Robert Dahl, and Mark Tushnet.

Reforming this system will not be easy. The Supreme Court's power is deeply entrenched, and those who benefit from it—including the legal establishment that has grown up around judicial review—will resist change. But the time has come to have a serious national conversation about whether the United States should continue to be governed, in crucial respects, by an unelected committee of nine. The principle that the people should govern themselves is too important to leave to the discretion of judges appointed by presidents and confirmed by senators in a process that has come to resemble, more than anything else, a Byzantine ritual of court intrigue.

A constitutional order worthy of a democratic republic is one in which the people themselves, through their elected representatives or their direct votes, have the final say on the meaning of their fundamental charter. The Supreme Court as we know it should be abolished, and a more democratic system of constitutional interpretation put in its place.

The following summarizes arguments made by various constitutional scholars, legal academics, and political figures across the ideological spectrum who advocate for significant changes to or elimination of the Supreme Court's power of judicial review. These remain minority positions in mainstream legal thought but are supported by substantive scholarship.

Core Arguments

1. The Democratic Deficit

Proponents argue that the Supreme Court is structurally undemocratic in several ways:

  • Unelected and unaccountable: Justices are appointed, not elected, and serve for life, insulating them from public opinion.
  • Reversing majority will: Nine individuals can invalidate laws passed by elected representatives and signed by a directly elected president.
  • The "countermajoritarian difficulty": Legal scholar Alexander Bickel coined this term to describe the tension between judicial review and democratic self-governance. Critics argue this is not just a difficulty but a fundamental flaw.

Scholars such as Jeremy Waldron (NYU) have argued that legislatures are better positioned to deliberate on rights questions because they are democratically accountable and their members face public scrutiny.

2. Judicial Review Is Not Constitutionally Explicit

The power of judicial review—the Court's authority to strike down laws as unconstitutional—was established in Marbury v. Madison (1803), not explicitly granted in the Constitution. Critics contend:

  • The Framers did not intend for the Court to have this power.
  • Larry Kramer, former dean of Stanford Law School, argued in The People Themselves (2004) that early American practice centered on popular constitutionalism, with elected legislatures, not courts, as the primary interpreters.
  • The Constitution's Article V amendment process and Supremacy Clause suggest legislative interpretation was meant to be more central.

3. Perceived Politicization

Reform advocates argue that justices frequently decide cases based on political ideology rather than neutral legal reasoning:

  • Empirical studies show justices often vote along predictable ideological lines.
  • Confirmation hearings have become increasingly contentious partisan battles.
  • Decisions on contested issues (abortion, gun rights, campaign finance) appear to track the appointing president's party.
  • This undermines the claim that courts offer a uniquely neutral forum for constitutional questions.

4. Life Tenure Concerns

Lifetime appointments raise specific problems:

  • Justices may serve 30+ years, during which societal views evolve dramatically.
  • Justices can remain in office long past the point of diminished capacity.
  • The original rationale (independence from political pressure) may no longer justify the costs in a politicized environment.

5. Representation and Legitimacy

Critics argue the Court fails to represent the American population:

  • Historically, the Court has lacked diversity in race, gender, and background.
  • Nine justices from a nation of 330 million people may not adequately reflect the breadth of American society and perspectives.
  • Democratic mechanisms, by contrast, would draw legitimacy from popular participation.

Proposed Democratic Alternatives

Various replacement mechanisms have been proposed, ranging from modest reforms to complete restructuring:

Parliamentary Supremacy

  • The British model, where Parliament is the ultimate authority on constitutional questions and courts cannot strike down primary legislation.
  • Would require either a constitutional amendment or a fundamental shift in how courts interpret their own authority.

Congressional Supermajority Override

  • Allow Congress to override Supreme Court decisions with a supermajority (e.g., two-thirds vote).
  • Preserves judicial review but places final authority with elected representatives.

"Balanced Rollover" or Super-Legislature

  • A proposal (associated with Akhil Amar and others) where a panel of elected officials or a special body reviews and can override judicial decisions.

Term Limits and Elections

  • Replace life tenure with fixed terms (e.g., 18 years as one reform proposal suggests).
  • Implement direct or indirect elections for justices.
  • Would preserve the Court but change its democratic character.

Sunsetting Decisions

  • Court decisions would expire after a set period (e.g., 20 years) unless reaffirmed.
  • Forces periodic re-examination and allows evolving democratic consensus to prevail.

Popular Constitutionalism

  • Empower citizens directly through ballot initiatives, constitutional conventions, or popular ratification of judicial decisions.
  • This is closer to how some state constitutions operate.

Random Selection

  • Draw justices from a pool of qualified legal professionals by lottery.
  • Reduces political selection while maintaining expertise.

Scholarly Support

Notable scholars who have advanced versions of these arguments include:

  • Jeremy Waldron (NYU) – argues rights are better protected by democratic deliberation.
  • Larry Kramer (Stanford) – argues the Framers intended popular constitutionalism.
  • Sanford Levinson (University of Texas) – has questioned the Court's legitimacy and structure.
  • Akhil Amar (Yale) – has proposed various democratic reform mechanisms.
  • Mark Tushnet (Harvard) – has advocated "weak-form" judicial review and greater legislative primacy.
  • Richard Epstein (NYU/Hoover) – has critiqued the Court from a classical liberal perspective.

The Counterargument (Briefly)

It is worth noting the orthodox defense of judicial review, as proponents of abolition are rebutting an established tradition. Defenders argue that:

  • The Court protects minority rights against majority tyranny.
  • Courts provide neutral, principled interpretation immune from political pressure.
  • Marbury v. Madison has been settled law for over 220 years and forms part of the constitutional system.
  • Democratic mechanisms historically produced worse outcomes for marginalized groups (e.g., Jim Crow laws, which the Court eventually helped dismantle).
  • Constitutional democracies worldwide vary, but many stable democracies (Germany, Canada, India) maintain strong judicial review.

Conclusion

Proponents of reform or abolition generally argue that constitutional interpretation is too important to be left to nine unelected individuals, and that democratic accountability, while imperfect, offers a more legitimate foundation for resolving fundamental legal disputes. They view judicial review as a historically contingent development rather than a sacred feature of American government, and they believe alternative institutional designs could better balance stability, expertise, and democratic legitimacy. These arguments remain contested and represent a minority position in American legal culture, which has generally accepted the Court's role for over two centuries.

Let us speak plainly about what we have allowed to be built in our name.

A government of laws, not of kings—that was the cry of our Revolution. And yet we permit a body of nine, sitting for life, with no obligation to face a single voter, to strike down the laws our elected representatives pass, the executives we elect sign, and the deliberations of our democratic process produce. We call this freedom. We call this a republic. I call it a contradiction at the heart of our house that we have refused to confront.

Consider what this has wrought.

In 1857, seven justices—seven unelected lawyers—told nearly four million human beings that they could be owned like cattle, that their chains were constitutional, that the hopes of their mothers and the prayers of their children were nothing before the property rights of their masters. Dred Scott was the law of the land until a war had to be fought to wash it away.

In 1896, this same Court blessed the segregation of streetcars, the separation of human beings into the degraded and the superior, and called it equal. Plessy stood for sixty years, defended by those same robes, until a new generation of justices finally acknowledged what should never have required acknowledgment: that injustice dressed in legal language is still injustice.

In the early twentieth century, the Court spent a generation striking down minimum wage laws, child labor restrictions, limits on working hours—each time wrapping its rulings in the soaring language of "liberty" and "freedom of contract," while six-year-old children worked in mills and workers died in factories for wages that could not feed them. Theodore Roosevelt, the great progressive, was right to thunder that the Court had become a body of "nine old men" standing athwart the democratic hopes of the people.

And what have we done? We have refined the absurdity. We have created a system in which vacancies are filled by presidents who win elections by margins so thin they could be reversed by a single sneeze, in which senators representing a fraction of the population can blockade a nomination for years, in which justices are selected not for wisdom but for their predictions about how they will rule on the great controversies of our age. We have built a system in which the most consequential decisions about our common life are made by people we cannot hire, cannot fire, cannot recall, and cannot remove except through a process so cumbersome it has been used successfully exactly once in our entire history.

This is not a judiciary. This is a cloistered aristocracy of the law, and it has outlived its legitimacy.

I hear the objections. Who will guard the Constitution if not the courts? But this question assumes the answer to itself. The Constitution belongs to the people who wrote it, who ratified it, and who have amended it fifteen times—yes, through the most democratic of our processes. The Constitution is a covenant among the living, not a sacred text to be guarded by priests in robes.

But the people might make mistakes! Of course they might. So might judges. The question is not whether mistakes will be made, but who has the legitimate authority to make them, and who must bear the consequences. When the legislature errs, the legislature can be turned out. When a president errs, the president can be voted out. When the Court errs, the Court waits for death, resignation, or a slow grinding of years. The democratic process can correct itself. The Court cannot, and will not, until enough justices die and enough new ones are confirmed.

But the protection of minorities! We are told that the Court stands between the people and their worst impulses. And yet for two hundred years this Court has blessed slavery, segregation, the crushing of labor, the internment of Japanese Americans, the denial of citizenship to women, the criminalization of contraception, the gutting of voting rights, and on and on and on, often decades after the people had already moved past those moral outrages. The Court has not stood as a shield for minorities; it has stood as a shield for the comfortable, against the demanding, until the demanding grew too large to ignore.

What do I propose?

I propose that we return constitutional interpretation to where it belongs: to the people themselves, acting through their elected representatives, through the democratic process that alone carries legitimate authority in a self-governing society. I propose that the final word on what our Constitution means be spoken not by nine lawyers insulated in marble chambers, but by the citizens whose lives those words are meant to govern.

Some will say this is radical. It is not. It is the oldest position in our tradition. It was the position of Thomas Jefferson, who wrote that the Constitution itself should expire every nineteen years, that no generation could bind another. It was the position of Andrew Jackson, who reportedly said of Worcester v. Georgia: "John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it." It was the position of Lincoln, who said that no Court could make a man a slave if the people had decided otherwise. It was the position of the populist movement of the late nineteenth century, of the labor movement, of the civil rights movement when it was young and unafraid. It is the position of every democracy on earth that does not surrender the meaning of its fundamental law to a committee of lawyers.

I am not asking you to break the Constitution. I am asking you to reclaim it. I am asking you to remember that the first three words of that document are not "We, the Judges." They are "We, the People."

And what is the alternative? To continue accepting that our most important decisions—about who counts as a person, about what rights we possess, about the boundaries of state power, about the meaning of equality and liberty themselves—are to be made by a body whose members are selected by political horse-trading, who serve for life, who face no electoral consequence, and who, when they err, do not pay the price for their errors, but pass them on to generations not yet born?

How long will we say, in the same breath, that this is a democracy, and that nine unelected people have the final say?

How long will we accept that the most powerful office in this country is one that cannot be voted out of, cannot be voted in, and was never given to the people by the people?

The answer, I tell you, is that we have tolerated it for too long already. The answer is that the people of this country are waking up. The answer is that a system which produces the corruption, the partisanship, the lifetime tenure, and the brazen political behavior we now witness from our highest Court has lost its claim to our reverence.

I do not ask for revolution in the streets. I ask for revolution in the mind—the quiet, steady, democratic revolution of citizens who have remembered what they were always supposed to know: that no institution, however ancient, however hallowed, however often invoked, is above the people who created it.

The Court is not the Constitution. The Court is not the country. The Court is not the sovereign.

We are.

And the time has come to act like it.

Thank you, and may God bless the people of the United States—all three hundred and thirty million of them, and not one more, and not one less, than the rest.

Title: Toward Democratic Sovereignty: Why the Supreme Court Should Be Abolished

The United States Supreme Court, often viewed as the final arbiter of constitutional interpretation, holds immense unchecked power over the nation’s laws and policies. However, this unelected body, with lifetime tenure and near-absolute authority, undermines democratic principles and the will of the people. It is time to reimagine governance by abolishing the Supreme Court and eliminating judicial review, substituting this outdated institution with a system where elected representatives and popular votes determine the meaning of the Constitution. Through this reform, the United States can reclaim its democratic essence, ensure accountability, and adapt its foundational document to evolving societal values.

Judicial Review: A Flawed Innovation Beyond the Framers’ Intent

Judicial review—the power of courts to invalidate laws conflicting with the Constitution—was not explicitly established by the Founding Fathers. It was a controversial judicial creation in Marlow v. Madison (1803), controversially justified as a necessary check on legislative overreach. Yet James Madison, the Constitution’s architect, later called this move a “misconstruction” of the document. The framers envisioned a dynamic balance of power among co-equal branches, with Congress holding the primary role in constitutional lawmaking. By granting unelected judges the ultimate say in constitutional interpretation, the Supreme Court has overstepped its bounds, usurping a authority that belongs to the people’s elected representatives.

The Tyranny of the Judiciary

Unaccountable to the public, Supreme Court justices serve for life, insulated from the consequences of their rulings. In contrast, elected lawmakers must face re-election and public scrutiny. This disconnect fuels a “judicial tyranny,” where ideologically driven decisions defy the preferences of the majority. The Court’s 2010 Citizens United ruling, which equated money with speech, exemplifies this disconnect: billions of dollars in dark money have since flooded elections, distorting democracy while justices retire to comfortable obscurity. Similarly, in 2022, the overturning of Roe v. Wade sparked nationwide protests, revealing how the Court’s abstract “originalism” can override widely held beliefs about bodily autonomy. When judges, not the people, decide the fate of rights and liberties, democracy erodes.

Democratic Legitimacy Over Legal Elitism

Democracy thrives on transparency, participation, and answerability—principles absent in judicial supremacy. Elected legislators, though imperfect, reflect the will of the people and remain accountable to them. If citizens disagree with a law, their representatives can be voted out. This process ensures that constitutional values evolve with society, adapting to new realities rather than clinging to 18th-century understandings. The American public, through ballot initiatives and referendums, often successfully challenges controversial laws directly. In 2020, for instance, 15 states legalized marijuana via popular vote, defying decades of federal inaction. Abolishing judicial review would empower such democratic processes, granting the people greater agency over their own governance.

Addressing Counterarguments: Protecting Rights and Checks and Balances

Critics argue that removing judicial review would leave vulnerable populations at the mercy of the majority. However, democracy’s strength lies in its institutional redundancies: federalism dilutes centralized power, a free press exposes injustice, and elected officials can still champion civil rights. Moreover, unchecked majoritarianism is a myth—constitutional amendments, which require supermajorities, already act as a safeguard. The Civil Rights Acts of the 20th century, passed by Congress despite resistance, prove that legislative bodies can and do protect minority interests.

The concern that Congress might fail to self-regulate is valid but manageable. Expanding the role of state courts and federal prosecutors in defending constitutional rights could serve as interim checks. Additionally, empowering juries and introducing citizen panels for constitutional questions would distribute interpretation across diverse voices, reducing the risk of elite bias.

Conclusion: A Constitutional Renaissance

Abolishing the Supreme Court and judicial review is not radical—it is a return to the democratic ideals enshrined in the Constitution’s preamble: a government “of the people, by the people, for the people.” This reform would restore sovereignty to the electorate, ensuring that constitutional interpretation reflects contemporary values and remains accountable to the public. While change may seem daunting, the current system’s failures—from partisan gridlock to judicial overreach—underscore its fragility. It is time to trust democracy over judicial dictatorship. By choosing this path, America can forge a more responsive and legitimate union, where the Constitution grows with the people it serves.

The Supreme Court’s legacy is one of inequality and entrenched elite power. Its abolition is a necessary step toward a fairer, more democratic future. The question is not whether we can afford to act—it is whether we can afford not to.

  • Increased Democratic Accountability: Critics argue that unelected justices wield excessive influence over policy, bypassing the will of elected representatives and the public.   • Reduced Partisan Entrenchment: The current system of appointing justices can lead to ideologically polarized courts, as presidents choose nominees based on party preferences. 2. Reasons for Reform (or Abolition)

  • Undemocratic Nature of Judicial Review: Established in Marbury v. Madison (1803), judicial review allows the Court to invalidate laws or executive actions it deems unconstitutional. Opponents argue this grants unelected judges a form of "supreme" lawmaking authority, undermining the principle that elected branches should have final say on public policy.
  • Lack of Accountability and Transparency: Lifetime tenure insulates justices from political and electoral consequences, which some view as problematic.   • Potential Judicial Overreach: Critics often cite instances where the Court has overturned legislative or popular initiatives (e.g., decisions on voting rights, LGBTQ+ protections, or environmental regulations) as evidence of judicial activism. They argue this can stifle democratic progress and public will.
  • Precedential Rigidity: The Court’s authority to enshrine rulings as binding precedent can lead to prolonged adherence to outdated interpretations, particularly when societal norms shift. A democratic reinterpretation process could allow for more adaptable constitutional evolution.

3. Proposed Democratic Alternatives

  • Term-Limited Courts: Replacing lifetime tenure with fixed terms (e.g., 10-year terms, staggered elections) could reduce the stakes of individual appointments and encourage regular renewal of judicial perspectives.
  • Legislative Interpretation: Advocates might propose empowering Congress to have the final say on constitutional issues, either through specialized committees or supermajority votes. This would prioritize elected representatives’ deliberations over judicial fiat.
  • Citizen Assemblies or Conventions: Structured deliberative bodies of randomly selected citizens could periodically review constitutional interpretation, similar to practices in some democracies (e.g., citizen panels in Ireland or Canada). This approach seeks to blend public opinion with expert-informed discussion.
  • Regional or State-Based Solutions: In a federal system, critics of Supreme Court supremacy sometimes argue for decentralizing constitutional interpretation, letting states or regional councils handle issues tailored to their unique contexts.
  • Popular Referendums: Direct democracy mechanisms (e.g., ballot initiatives or referendums) could allow voters to ratify or reject constitutional decisions, particularly on divisive social or policy issues.

4. Counterarguments and Considerations

Opponents of abolishing the Court highlight potential risks of such reforms:

  • Erosion of Checks and Balances: The Court serves as an independent check on majority rule; removing it might weaken protections for minority rights and individual liberties from legislative overreach.
  • Instability and Conflict: Frequent constitutional reinterpretation by shifting majorities could lead to policy volatility and legal uncertainty, undermining the rule of law.
  • Tyranny of the Majority: Democratic mechanisms might prioritize the preferences of dominant political coalitions over enduring constitutional principles or minority interests.

5. Broader Implications

Proponents of reform often frame their arguments within broader debates about democratic legitimacy. They emphasize values like inclusivity, adaptability, and popular sovereignty, while critics stress the importance of judicial independence as a safeguard against fleeting majorities. The tension reflects differing visions of how to balance efficiency, stability, and democratic participation in a large, diverse nation.

Conclusion

The debate over abolishing the Supreme Court or curbing judicial review centers on fundamental questions about governance: Who should interpret the Constitution, and how should its meaning evolve over time? Advocates argue for democratizing this process to reflect modern values and reduce institutional rigidity, while others warn such changes could destabilize constitutional protections and invite majority tyranny. This discussion remains ongoing, with proponents of reform often citing historical dissatisfaction with courts (e.g., during the New Deal era or ongoing polarization) and pointing to alternative models in other democracies. Any significant structural change would require profound constitutional or legislative restructuring and could reshape the U.S. system’s long-standing balance of power.

Introduction

The United States Supreme Court, established by Article III of the Constitution, has long been considered the final arbiter of constitutional law. However, the principle of judicial review, which grants the Court the power to interpret the Constitution and declare laws unconstitutional, has become increasingly contentious. The Problem with Judicial Review

The primary issue with the current system is the lack of democratic accountability. The Supreme Court is composed of nine justices, appointed for life, who are not directly accountable to the electorate. This means that their interpretations of the Constitution can override the will of the people, as expressed through their elected representatives. This is particularly problematic when the Court strikes down laws passed by Congress or state legislatures, or when it interprets the Constitution in ways that contradict the will of the majority.

Moreover, the Supreme Court's interpretation of the Constitution has often been criticized for being overly broad and subjective. Justices are not bound by precedent in the same way that legislators are bound by the will of the people. This leads to a system where a small group of unelected officials can impose their own interpretation of the Constitution on the entire nation.

The Case for Representative Democracy

In contrast, a system where constitutional interpretation is determined by elected representatives or popular vote would be more democratic and accountable. Here are several reasons why this would be beneficial:

  1. Accountability: Elected representatives are directly accountable to the people. They must stand for re-election and can be voted out of office if their constituents disagree with their interpretations of the Constitution. This ensures that the will of the people is reflected in constitutional law.

  2. Transparency: The process of constitutional interpretation would be more transparent. Elected representatives would debate and vote on constitutional issues in public, allowing for greater scrutiny and input from the electorate.

  3. Flexibility: A system where constitutional interpretation is determined by elected representatives or popular vote would be more flexible. It would allow for changes to the Constitution to keep up with the evolving needs and values of society.

  4. Reducing Partisan Polarization: The Supreme Court's decisions have often been seen as partisan, with justices aligning with one political party or another. A system where constitutional interpretation is determined by elected representatives or popular vote could help to reduce this polarization, as elected officials would be more likely to consider the views of their constituents from all political parties.

A Possible Alternative: Popular Initiatives

One possible alternative to the Supreme Court is a system of popular initiatives. This would allow citizens to propose and vote on constitutional amendments directly. While this would not eliminate the need for elected representatives entirely, it would give the people a direct say in constitutional law.

Conclusion

The United States Supreme Court and the principle of judicial review have long been considered sacrosanct. However, the lack of democratic accountability and the subjective nature of constitutional interpretation make a strong case for their abolition. A system where constitutional interpretation is determined by elected representatives or popular vote would be more democratic, accountable, transparent, flexible, and less prone to partisan polarization. It is time to consider a new approach to constitutional law that reflects the will of the people.

Alexander Hamilton, in Federalist 78, argued for judicial independence to protect the Constitution from transient legislative majorities, but he never envisioned an unelected body overriding the permanent will of the people expressed through their representatives on fundamental constitutional principles. The doctrine was invented de facto by Chief Justice John Marshall in Marbury v. The core argument against judicial review is its blatant contradiction of democratic principles. Whether one agrees or disagrees with the outcomes, the mechanism is the problem: Constitutional meaning, defining the very boundaries of our rights and government, should not rest on the narrow margins of a single case argued before an unrepresentative panel. The Case for Abolishing Judicial Supremacy: A Thought Experiment in Democratic Constitutionalism

Note: The following essay presents one side of a longstanding debate for intellectual exploration. It does not represent my personal endorsement of abolishing the U.S. Supreme Court, which would raise profound practical and constitutional challenges. I offer it as requested—a rigorous examination of arguments that scholars, activists, and political thinkers have raised over centuries.

Introduction

In 1803, Chief Justice John Marshall seized a power that the Constitution never explicitly granted. In Marbury v. Madison, the Supreme Court declared for itself the authority to strike down acts of Congress, establishing the principle of judicial review. For more than two centuries, nine unelected, lifetime-appointed justices have exercised what amounts to final say over the meaning of the most consequential document in American governance. This arrangement, defenders argue, is the guardian of liberty. But a careful examination reveals it to be something far more troubling: a fundamentally undemocratic institution that concentrates extraordinary power in the hands of people who answer to no one, that has historically obstructed justice as often as it has advanced it, and that distorts the very constitutional republic it claims to protect.

The argument presented here is not that courts should have no role, or that the rule of law is unimportant. Rather, it is that this particular arrangement—lifetime-appointed judges wielding veto power over the democratic process—is neither the only nor the best way to protect rights or interpret a constitution. There are serious alternatives worth considering, and honest engagement with this idea strengthens democratic thinking regardless of where one ultimately lands.

I. The Counter-Majoritarian Problem: Rule by the Few Over the Many

The most fundamental objection to judicial supremacy is elegantly simple: it is rule by people no one elected and no one can remove.

Alexander Hamilton, in Federalist No. 78, described the judiciary as the "least dangerous branch," possessing "neither force nor will, but merely judgment." History has proven this assessment spectacularly wrong. The Supreme Court has become arguably the most consequential branch of government. A single ruling can reshape the lives of 330 million people—on healthcare, voting rights, marriage, criminal justice, campaign finance, gun policy, and abortion—without a single vote being cast by any representative of the public.

Consider the composition of the Court today. Nine justices are selected through a deeply politicized process where a president (who may have lost the popular vote) nominates candidates who are confirmed by a Senate where Wyoming's 580,000 residents have the same representation as California's 39 million. Once confirmed, these justices serve for life—average tenures now exceed 25 years—meaning that a justice confirmed at age 50 may shape American law into their late seventies or beyond, long after the political coalition that elevated them has dissolved.

Defenders of this system argue that insulation from democratic pressure is a feature, not a bug—that it allows justices to protect unpopular minorities from majoritarian tyranny. This argument deserves serious engagement, but it contains a hidden and troubling assumption: that the judgment of nine lawyers is more trustworthy than the collective judgment of the democratic process. This is, at its core, an argument against self-governance.

II. The Historical Record: A Mixed Bag at Best

Proponents of judicial review often point to Brown v. Board of Education (1954) and Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) as proof that the Court protects minorities. But this selective reading of history obscures a far more complicated—and often damning—record.

The Court as Obstacle to Justice

For most of American history, the Supreme Court has been a conservative institution in the structural sense—one that has more frequently blocked progressive change than advanced it.

  • Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857): The Court declared that Black people "had no rights which the white man was bound to respect," enshrining slavery into constitutional law and helping precipitate the Civil War.

  • Plessy v. Ferguson (1896): The Court sanctioned racial segregation for nearly six decades.

  • Lochner v. New York (1905): The Court struck down labor protections, minimum wage laws, and child labor restrictions for a generation during the Gilded Age, enforcing a laissez-faire ideology nowhere found in the Constitution's text.

  • Korematsu v. United States (1944): The Court upheld the internment of 120,000 Japanese Americans—citizens stripped of their liberty based on ethnicity.

  • Citizens United v. FEC (2010): The Court struck down campaign finance restrictions, opening the floodgates to unlimited corporate spending in elections, effectively amplifying the power of wealth in a democratic system.

  • Shelby County v. Holder (2013): The Court gutted the Voting Rights Act of 1965—arguably the most important piece of civil rights legislation in American history—leading to a wave of voter suppression laws across the country.

The uncomfortable truth is this: the Court that decided Brown is the same institution that decided Plessy. The justices who protected voting rights in the 1960s are the same institution that gutted those protections in 2013. The system has no inherent progressive direction. It reflects, at any given moment, the ideology of whoever happens to occupy the bench.

The Problem of Reversal Without Accountability

When a legislature passes a bad law, voters can replace the legislators. When the Court issues a bad ruling, the only remedies are constitutional amendment (an extraordinarily difficult process requiring supermajorities in Congress and state legislatures) or waiting decades for the Court to reverse itself. Plessy stood for 58 years. The Lochner era persisted for roughly four decades. Real people suffered real harm during those periods, with no democratic recourse.

This is not a minor design flaw. It is a structural feature that makes the system unresponsive to the evolving moral understanding of the citizenry.

III. Originalism vs. Living Constitutionalism: A Debate That Proves the Problem

The legal academy is consumed by a debate between two theories of constitutional interpretation. Originalists argue the Constitution should be interpreted according to its original public meaning at the time of ratification. Living constitutionalists argue it should be interpreted in light of evolving values and contemporary circumstances.

But here is the critical insight: the very existence of this unresolved debate demonstrates the problem with judicial review. If reasonable, intelligent legal scholars cannot agree on how the Constitution should be interpreted after more than two centuries of argument, why should we entrust the final answer to nine people selected through a partisan process?

Under an originalist framework, the meaning of the Constitution is fixed by the understanding of men who owned slaves, who did not believe women should vote, and who lived in a world without electricity, the internet, nuclear weapons, or global supply chains. Under a living constitutionalist framework, the meaning of the Constitution is effectively whatever the current justices say it is—a remarkably subjective exercise dressed in the language of legal reasoning.

In practice, justices routinely reach conclusions that align with their prior political and ideological commitments. Empirical studies consistently show that judicial decision-making correlates strongly with the appointing president's party. The "law" the Court applies is, in significant part, politics by other means.

IV. The Democratic Alternative: Popular Constitutionalism

The United States is nearly alone among mature democracies in granting its judiciary such unchecked power. While many democracies have constitutional courts, few grant them the same combination of lifetime tenure, unreviewable authority, and broad jurisdiction that characterizes the U.S. Supreme Court.

Several alternatives deserve serious consideration:

A. Legislative Supremacy in Constitutional Interpretation

Under this model—common in parliamentary democracies like the United Kingdom until relatively recently—elected legislatures bear primary responsibility for interpreting constitutional principles. The British system operated for centuries without judicial review of parliamentary sovereignty, and the UK developed robust rights protections through legislative action, political culture, and common law evolution.

Advocates argue that legislators who must face the voters are more likely to reflect the actual values of the community than judges accountable to no one. When legislatures err, the public has recourse. When courts err, the public must wait—sometimes for generations.

B. Supermajoritarian Legislative Override

A more moderate approach would preserve judicial review but allow elected legislatures to override Court decisions with a supermajority vote—similar to Canada's "notwithstanding clause" in Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This preserves judicial input while ensuring that the final word belongs to democratic institutions.

This model recognizes that courts may sometimes be right to push back against majority overreach, but denies them the last word. The people, through their representatives, retain ultimate authority.

C. Popular Constitutional Conventions

"Without the Court, minorities would be oppressed."

This is the most powerful argument for judicial review, and it deserves respect. But it rests on the historically dubious assumption that the Court has been a reliable protector of minorities. As the record above demonstrates, the Court has been as likely to oppress minorities as to protect them. The real drivers of minority rights in America have been social movements, legislative action, and constitutional amendments—not judicial fiat. The Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments were products of a civil war and democratic politics. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 were products of mass mobilization and legislative courage. The Court ratified these changes only after democratic movements made them politically inevitable.

Moreover, the argument proves too much. If we cannot trust the democratic process to protect rights, then the answer is to strengthen democratic institutions, not to replace them with aristocratic ones. Judicial supremacy is a bandage over a wound it cannot heal.

This claim is historically contested. The Constitution's text says nothing about judicial review. Marshall's argument in Marbury was an inference—a creative one, critics would say—from the structure of the document. The Framers debated extensively and rejected proposals to give the judiciary a formal veto over legislation. James Madison's original proposals at the Constitutional Convention included a "Council of Revision" that would have given judges a role in reviewing legislation—but alongside the executive and with the possibility of legislative override. The Convention rejected even this modest proposal.

The idea that the Framers intended unlimited, unreviewable judicial supremacy is a myth constructed after the fact.

"Majorities can be tyrannical."

Yes, they can. But so can minorities—and unelected judges are a minority. The question is not whether power can be abused; it can be, regardless of where it resides. The question is which arrangement provides the most accountability and self-correction. Democratic systems, for all their flaws, have built-in mechanisms for correction: elections, free speech, free press, political organization. Judicial supremacy has almost none.

VI. The Deeper Philosophical Question

At the heart of this debate is a question about the nature of democracy itself. Do we trust the people to govern themselves?

If the answer is yes—if we believe, as Lincoln articulated, that government "of the people, by the people, for the people" is the highest aspiration of political life—then we must grapple honestly with the fact that judicial review places final authority over the most important questions in the hands of people who are emphatically not of the people, not chosen by the people, and not accountable to the people.

The philosopher Jeremy Bentham argued that all political authority ultimately derives from the consent of the governed. John Stuart Mill contended that the best safeguard against tyranny is the active, ongoing engagement of citizens in their own governance. Both thinkers would have viewed the American system of judicial supremacy with deep suspicion—not because they opposed rights, but because they understood that rights secured without democratic participation are fragile, contingent on the goodwill of their guardians, and ultimately unsustainable.

The history of American constitutionalism bears this out. The most durable expansions of rights have come through democratic struggle—the abolition of slavery, women's suffrage, labor rights, civil rights—while the Court has oscillated between advancing and retarding these causes according to the temperaments of its members.

VII. Practical Steps Toward Reform

For those persuaded that reform is needed, several incremental steps could move the system in a more democratic direction:

  1. Constitutional amendment establishing legislative override of judicial review with a two-thirds supermajority in both chambers of Congress, subject to presidential signature or veto override.

  2. Term limits for Supreme Court justices (18 years has been widely proposed), ensuring regular turnover and reducing the stakes of any single appointment.

  3. Expansion of the Court to dilute the outsized influence of any single justice and reduce the partisan intensity of confirmation battles.

  4. Establishment of a Constitutional Interpretation Commission composed of elected representatives, legal scholars, and citizen delegates, charged with providing authoritative—but non-binding—interpretive guidance.

  5. Greater use of popular referenda on constitutional questions at the state level, building institutional capacity for direct democratic participation in constitutional meaning.

Conclusion

The American system of judicial supremacy is not written in stone. It was invented by a chief justice in 1803, expanded through practice over two centuries, and defended by those who benefit from it. It has produced moments of genuine justice and moments of profound injustice. It concentrates extraordinary power in the hands of people who are unelected, unaccountable, and serve for life. It has repeatedly blocked the will of democratic majorities on questions of fundamental rights and social policy, and it has repeatedly failed to protect those same rights when they most needed protection.

The alternative—a system where constitutional meaning is shaped by the people and their elected representatives—is not utopian. It is the norm in most of the democratic world. It is grounded in the radical but essential idea that people are capable of governing themselves, that democratic deliberation is not merely a means to an end but a good in itself, and that the legitimacy of a constitution ultimately depends not on the pronouncements of nine lawyers but on the ongoing consent and active participation of the governed.

The question is not whether we should have rights—we should. The question is who gets to define and enforce them, and whether that authority should rest with the people or with a self-perpetuating aristocracy of legal elites. The answer, for anyone who takes democracy seriously, should be clear.

Thoughtful people can and do disagree on these questions.

Abolish the Supreme Court: Restoring Democratic Sovereignty over Constitutional Interpretation

In 2022, the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, eliminating the constitutional right to abortion that had been recognized for nearly half a century. The Anti-Democratic Nature of Judicial Review

At the heart of American democracy lies the principle that those who govern must be accountable to the governed. Yet the Supreme Court stands as a glaring exception. Its nine members are appointed for life, answerable to no electorate, and virtually immune from removal. Through judicial review—first asserted in Marbury v. Madison (1803)—the Court claims the power to nullify any law enacted by Congress or the states that it deems unconstitutional. In effect, a handful of unelected individuals can veto the will of millions of voters as expressed through their representatives. This is not democracy; it is oligarchy dressed in black robes.

The framers of the Constitution never explicitly granted the judiciary this sweeping authority. Indeed, the Constitution is silent on judicial review. The doctrine was invented by the Court itself in a politically motivated decision that Chief Justice John Marshall used to expand the judiciary’s power. Thomas Jefferson, a principal author of the Declaration of Independence, warned that “the Constitution is a mere thing of wax in the hands of the judiciary, which they may twist and shape into any form they please.” Jefferson’s fears have been realized: the Court has repeatedly reshaped the Constitution according to its own ideological preferences, undermining the democratic process.

Politicization and the Erosion of Legitimacy

Far from being a neutral arbiter, the modern Supreme Court is a deeply politicized body. Justices are nominated by presidents and confirmed by senators based largely on their perceived ideological leanings. Once on the bench, they often decide cases along predictable partisan lines. From Bush v. Gore (2000), which decided a presidential election, to Citizens United v. FEC (2010), which unleashed unlimited corporate spending in elections, to Shelby County v. Holder (2013), which gutted the Voting Rights Act, the Court’s rulings have consistently advanced a conservative agenda. The recent overturning of Roe v. Wade in Dobbs v. Jackson (2022) was the culmination of a decades-long campaign by Republicans to install justices who would deliver a specific policy outcome.

This blatant politicization has shattered the Court’s legitimacy. Public confidence in the institution has plummeted; many Americans now view it as little more than a super-legislature, wielding enormous power without accountability. When the Court intervenes in hot-button issues like abortion, gun control, or healthcare, it fuels resentment and division. If constitutional interpretation is inherently political—and the current Court proves that it is—then it should be conducted by politically accountable officials, not by life-tenured jurists.

A Poor Record in Protecting Rights and Liberties

Proponents of judicial review often argue that an independent judiciary is essential to safeguard minority rights against majority tyranny. History tells a different story. The Supreme Court has a long and ignominious record of upholding oppression rather than preventing it. In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), the Court declared that African Americans could not be citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories, a decision that helped precipitate the Civil War. Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) sanctioned racial segregation under the guise of “separate but equal.” Korematsu v. United States (1944) endorsed the forced internment of Japanese Americans during World War II. More recently, in Bowers v. Hardwick (1986), the Court upheld laws criminalizing homosexuality.

Even when the Court has issued progressive rulings—such as Brown v. Board of Education (1954) or Obergefell v. Hodges (2015)—it has usually followed, not led, societal change. Brown came after decades of civil rights activism and was implemented only because of sustained political pressure. Landmark expansions of rights have more often come from democratic branches: the Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act were passed by Congress and signed by the President; the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, Fifteenth, and Nineteenth Amendments were ratified by the states. Conversely, the Court has frequently struck down laws that protected workers, consumers, and voters. The Lochner era saw the invalidation of minimum wage and child labor laws; more recently, the Court has crippled campaign finance reform and weakened voting rights protections.

The truth is that judicial review is as likely to entrench minority rule as to prevent it. Life tenure allows justices to impose the ideologies of past presidents long after the electorate has moved on. The current 6–3 conservative majority is the product of electoral flukes and strategic retirements, yet it wields outsized influence over American life. Rights are safest when they are embedded in the Constitution through amendments or defended by legislators who must face the voters, not when they depend on the whims of nine unelected judges.

If the Supreme Court and judicial review are abolished, how would constitutional interpretation be handled? The answer is simple: by the people and their elected representatives. Many democracies function without strong judicial review. The United Kingdom, for example, operates under the principle of parliamentary sovereignty; the legislature is the ultimate authority on the meaning of law, including constitutional matters. New Zealand and the Netherlands have similar systems. Switzerland frequently uses referenda to decide important constitutional questions. These nations enjoy robust protections for individual rights, demonstrating that judicial review is not a prerequisite for a free society.

In the United States, we could adopt a system of legislative supremacy, where Congress has the final say on whether a law is constitutional. The President already possesses a veto power that can be exercised on constitutional grounds; if Congress overrides that veto with a supermajority, the law would stand. Alternatively, we could establish a mechanism for national referenda on constitutional issues, allowing citizens to directly vote on matters like abortion rights, gun regulations, or campaign finance. This would be true popular constitutionalism—the idea that “We the People” should interpret our founding document.

Such a system would have several advantages. First, it would restore democratic legitimacy to constitutional decision-making. Laws and interpretations would reflect the will of the majority, as expressed through elections and votes. Second, it would reduce the toxic politicization of the judiciary, allowing courts to focus on interpreting statutes and resolving ordinary legal disputes without being drawn into partisan battles. Third, it would encourage civic engagement; when citizens know their votes directly shape the Constitution’s meaning, they are more likely to participate in the democratic process. Finally, it would allow the Constitution to evolve organically with societal values, rather than being frozen by the interpretations of long-dead justices.

Critics will raise two primary objections: first, that without judicial review, majority tyranny will trample minority rights; second, that the rule of law requires a neutral arbiter to resolve constitutional disputes. Both concerns are overstated.

As for minority rights, history shows that the Supreme Court has been an unreliable guardian. Moreover, the Constitution itself provides structural protections: the amendment process requires supermajorities, making it difficult to strip away fundamental rights. Rights enshrined in the Constitution—such as freedom of speech, religion, and due process—would remain, but their interpretation would be determined by Congress or the people. In a functioning democracy, minority rights are best protected by building broad coalitions and appealing to the conscience of the majority, as demonstrated by the civil rights movement. Regarding the rule of law, abolishing judicial review does not mean eliminating courts altogether. The judiciary would continue to interpret and apply statutes, adjudicate disputes, and ensure fair trials. Only the power to invalidate laws on constitutional grounds would be removed. For those who worry about interbranch conflicts or federal-state disputes, we could create a specialized constitutional council composed of elected officials or citizen representatives chosen by lot. This body could issue advisory opinions, but the final decision would rest with the legislature or the people. The key is that no unelected, life-tenured body would have a veto over democratic outcomes.

A Call to Action

Abolishing the Supreme Court and ending judicial review is a radical proposal, but radical problems demand radical solutions. The current system has produced a judiciary that is anti-democratic, politicized, and often hostile to the very rights it claims to protect. It is time to return the power of constitutional interpretation to its rightful owners: the American people and the representatives they elect.

The Seventeenth Amendment (direct election of senators) and the Nineteenth Amendment (women’s suffrage) were once considered unattainable, yet they were achieved through persistent popular movements. We must build a movement that demands democratic control over the Constitution. Let us begin that work today.

In the words of Abraham Lincoln, “this country, with its institutions, belongs to the people who inhabit it.” The Supreme Court has usurped that belonging for too long. By abolishing it and embracing a system of legislative supremacy or popular referenda, we can finally realize the promise of a government truly of, by, and for the people.

Abolish the Supreme Court: Restoring Democracy by Eliminating Judicial Review

Introduction

The United States Supreme Court, once hailed as a bulwark of justice, has become an unelected legislative body that undermines democracy by imposing judicial supremacy over elected representatives. The principle of judicial review, established in Marbury v. Madison (1803), grants the Court the power to strike down laws passed by Congress and enacted by state legislatures, effectively allowing nine unelected justices to override the will of the people. This concentration of power in the judiciary is undemocratic, unaccountable, and increasingly dangerous to the principles of self-governance. The Supreme Court should be abolished, and judicial review eliminated in favor of constitutional interpretation determined by elected representatives or through popular vote. This essay argues that such a system would restore democratic accountability, prevent judicial overreach, and ensure that the Constitution remains a living document shaped by the people, not by an unaccountable elite.

The Supreme Court’s Undemocratic Nature

The Supreme Court is fundamentally undemocratic in its structure and function. The justices are appointed for life—a lifetime tenure that insulates them from public accountability. Unlike elected officials, who are subject to regular elections and can be removed for poor performance, Supreme Court justices face no consequences for ideologically driven rulings, corruption, or incompetence. This lack of accountability allows justices to act as policymakers, rewriting laws under the guise of "constitutional interpretation."

For example, the Court’s 2022 decision in Dobbs v. Jackson, which overturned Roe v. Wade and returned abortion laws to the states, was not a neutral application of constitutional text but a politically motivated reversal of precedent. The ruling disregarded decades of settled law and public opinion, demonstrating how judicial review empowers the Court to impose its own policy preferences regardless of democratic consensus. If the people’s representatives had voted on abortion laws state by state, the outcome would have been more representative of the electorate’s will.

Furthermore, the appointment process is deeply flawed. Presidents nominate justices based on ideological agendas rather than judicial fitness, and the Senate confirmation process has devolved into partisan theater. The result is that the Court is not a neutral arbiter but a super-legislature whose decisions reflect the prevailing political winds of the moment. This politicization erodes public trust in the judiciary and undermines the legitimacy of its rulings.

Judicial Review as an Undemocratic Power Grab

Judicial review grants the Supreme Court the authority to nullify laws passed by democratically elected bodies, a power that was never explicitly granted in the Constitution. While Alexander Hamilton argued in Federalist No. 78 that the judiciary would be the "least dangerous branch," history has proven otherwise. The Court has repeatedly overstepped its intended role, striking down laws that were within Congress’s constitutional authority.

Consider Brown v. Board of Education (1954), a landmark case that ended racial segregation in public schools. While the decision was just and necessary, it was not a model of judicial restraint—it deliberately overruled Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), which had upheld segregation under the "separate but equal" doctrine. The Court’s intervention, though historically significant, set a precedent for judicial activism rather than deferring to the democratic process. If the issue had been left to state legislatures or a constitutional amendment, the debate over segregation might have been more contentively resolved.

Conversely, the Court has also blocked progressive reforms, such as in Shelby County v. Holder (2013), which gutted the Voting Rights Act by striking down protections for minority voters. This decision, justified under the guise of "states' rights," had the effect of disenfranchising millions. Such outcomes prove that judicial review does not guarantee justice—it guarantees the whims of an unelected elite.

A Democratic Alternative: Legislative and Popular Constitutional Interpretation

If the Supreme Court were abolished, two primary methods could replace it for interpreting the Constitution:

1. Constitutional Amendments by Elected Representatives

The most democratic way to interpret or amend the Constitution is through Article V’s amendment process. However, this has been nearly impossible in modern times due to high thresholds—requiring two-thirds of Congress and three-fourths of state legislatures. Nonetheless, instead of relying on judicial fiat, Congress should be empowered to clarify constitutional ambiguities through amendments. For example, if the Court misinterprets the Second Amendment (as in Bruen 2022), Congress could propose a constitutional amendment defining "well-regulated militia" and "bear arms" in modern terms.

2. Popular Vote on Constitutional Issues

Another democratic solution is direct democracy—allowing the American people to vote on constitutional matters. Some states already use ballot initiatives to pass laws, and a federal mechanism could be established where Congress or state legislatures refer constitutional questions to a national referendum. For instance, if the Court rules that a law violates the Constitution, Congress could bypass judicial review by putting the same question to a national vote. This would ensure that the people, not nine justices, have the final say.

3. Reliance on State Legislatures

Since many constitutional disputes involve federalism (e.g., abortion, gun rights), these matters could be left to state legislatures, where elected representatives directly accountable to voters make the final decisions. This would restore the original intent of the Constitution, which was designed to leave many policy questions to state governance.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals

Critics of abolishing judicial review argue that it is necessary to protect minority rights and prevent majoritarian tyranny. However, this concern is overstated. The Court has often failed to protect minorities—examples include Plessy v. Ferguson, Korematsu v. United States (upholding Japanese internment), and Citizens United v. If the people’s representatives are trusted to pass laws, they can also be trusted to protect minority rights through inclusive legislation—for example, anti-discrimination laws, voting rights protections, and labor regulations.

Another counterargument is that without judicial review, Congress could abuse its power by passing unconstitutional laws. However, this assumes that an unelected judiciary is more trustworthy than elected officials, which is demonstrably false given the Court’s partisan rulings. If Congress passes a law that clearly violates the Constitution (e.g., banning a religion), the people and state governments can challenge it in state courts or through political resistance. The risk of tyranny is not eliminated by judicial review—it is merely shifted from an unaccountable Court to an unaccountable legislature.

Finally, some argue that eliminating judicial review would lead to legal chaos. But chaos is already present in a system where nine people dictate the meaning of the Constitution. If Congress and state legislatures were responsible for constitutional interpretation, legal consensus would arise through democratic debate, not judicial decrees.

Conclusion: Restoring Democracy to the Constitution

The Supreme Court, with its power of judicial review, has become the most powerful and least accountable branch of government. By striking down democratically enacted laws, the Court subverts the will of the people and replaces elected representatives with an unelected elite. The solution is clear: abolish the Supreme Court as we know it and replace judicial review with a system where constitutional interpretation is determined by elected officials or through popular vote.

This change would restore democratic accountability, reduce judicial overreach, and ensure that the Constitution remains a document of the people, not of nine justices. The American experiment in self-governance was never meant to rely on a black-robed oligarchy making final decisions behind closed doors. True democracy requires that the ultimate authority rests with the people—not in the marble halls of the Supreme Court.

The Case for Abolishing the Supreme Court: Restoring Democracy Through Popular Constitutional Interpretation

Introduction

The United States Supreme Court, often revered as the "greatest legal institution in the world," has become a symbol of judicial overreach, political polarization, and undemocratic decision-making. For over two centuries, the Court has operated under the principle of judicial review—the power to strike down laws and executive actions it deems unconstitutional. The Problem with Judicial Review: An Undemocratic Power Grab

1. The Supreme Court is Unelected and Unaccountable

The most fundamental flaw of judicial review is that it grants nine unelected, lifetime-appointed judges the power to override the will of 535 elected legislators and 46 million voters. Unlike Congress or the presidency, Supreme Court justices face no electoral consequences for their rulings. A justice who strikes down a popular law—whether on abortion, gun rights, or voting rights—cannot be voted out of office. This lack of accountability makes the Court a permanent countermajoritarian institution, where a small group of elites can impose their vision of the Constitution on the entire nation.

  • Example: In Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (2022), the Court overturned Roe v. Wade, eliminating federal abortion protections. If the people had voted on this issue, the outcome might have been different—but they were denied that right.

2. Judicial Activism Overrides Democracy

The Supreme Court has repeatedly ignored democratic processes in favor of judicial policymaking. Instead of interpreting the Constitution as it was originally understood (originalism), many justices engage in living constitutionalism, rewriting the law based on their personal beliefs.

  • Example: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Court declared racial segregation unconstitutional—a decision that was morally correct but legally dubious, as the Constitution did not explicitly ban segregation. Yet, the Court imposed its will on the nation, bypassing legislative debate.
  • Example: In Obergefell v. Hodges (2015), the Court legalized same-sex marriage nationwide, despite the fact that 60% of Americans opposed it at the time (Gallup, 2015). The justices, not the people, decided that marriage equality was a constitutional right.

These rulings demonstrate that the Court does not merely interpret the Constitution—it rewrites it based on judicial preferences.

3. The Court is Politicized and Partisan

Contrary to the myth of judicial neutrality, the Supreme Court has become deeply politicized. Confirmation battles have turned into raw partisan warfare, with Senate confirmation votes often split along ideological lines.

  • Example: The confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett in 2020 came just eight days before the election, raising serious questions about judicial independence.
  • Example: The 2020 Census case (Trump v. Hawaii) saw the Court rule in favor of the Trump administration’s discriminatory policies, with Chief Justice Roberts writing that the president’s actions were "presumptively lawful."

1. Replace Judicial Review with Legislative or Popular Voting

Instead of allowing nine unelected judges to decide what is constitutional, constitutional questions should be resolved by:

  • Congress (Legislative Interpretation): The Constitution grants Congress the power to interpret and enforce its provisions (Article I, Section 8). If a law is challenged, Congress—not the Court—should have the final say.
  • Popular Referendum (Direct Democracy): For major constitutional questions (e.g., abortion, gun rights, voting laws), the people should have the final vote through national referendums or state-level ballot initiatives.

  • Accountability: Elected officials and voters must answer to the people, not the other way around.
  • Flexibility: The Constitution can evolve with public opinion, rather than being frozen in time by judicial fiat.
  • Transparency: Debates over constitutional meaning would occur in open legislative sessions or public votes, not in secret judicial chambers.

  • Is subject to recall elections if they overstep their authority.
  • Operates under strict originalist principles, with no power to create new constitutional rights.

Even this limited reform would reduce judicial tyranny by ensuring that constitutional interpreters are temporary and accountable.

The Framers never intended for the Supreme Court to have unlimited judicial review. In Marbury v.
